practices.label: Agent in the loop
practices.what: AI takes a first pass (review, triage, codegen) with a human confirming.
starter: An AI code-review or triage step on PRs
An eval/golden-test harness for AI-generated output
A clear human-confirmation checkpoint before merge

practices.label: AI process & harness
practices.what: Ad-hoc prompting becomes a repeatable, trustworthy part of how the team ships.
starter: Evals / golden tests for AI-generated output
A versioned prompt & agent library the team reuses
Agent runbooks for recurring tasks
A review gate / Definition-of-Done for AI changes

practices.label: Agent guidance (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md)
practices.what: Machine-readable project context so any AI contribution lands consistent and on-spec.
starter: Build & test commands (how to run, lint, and verify)
Architecture map — entry points, key modules, data flow
“Verify after every change” rules (run tests, typecheck)
Constraints the agent must never break (security, public API, conventions)
MCP servers / hooks / subagents in use, if any
One or two examples of a good change

practices.label: Architecture docs & ADRs
practices.what: Context both humans and agents can read — less re-explaining, better changes.
starter: A /docs folder with agent-readable architecture notes
ADRs capturing why key decisions were made
Onboarding / “how this repo works” entry point

practices.label: Supply-chain security
practices.what: The shift-left guardrail against the vulnerable or secret-leaking code AI can confidently produce.
starter: SAST (e.g. CodeQL/Semgrep) running on every PR
Dependency + secret scanning wired into CI (Dependabot/Snyk, gitleaks)
Container image scanning when you ship images
SBOM + signed, attested build artifacts (cosign/SLSA)

practices.label: Test discipline
practices.what: The guardrail that makes AI-generated changes safe to merge.
starter: A behavioral test suite covering critical paths
Tests runnable with one command (wired into CI)
A “write/extend a test with every change” norm
Coverage visible enough to spot gaps

practices.label: Enforced quality
practices.what: Conventions held by tooling, not habit — slips caught at the earliest point.
starter: Linter + strict type settings, enforced in CI
Pre-commit / pre-push hooks
A PR template with a definition-of-done checklist

practices.label: CI gates on merge
practices.what: Trust that doesn't depend on which human reviewed — checks enforce it.
starter: Lint + typecheck + tests run on every PR
Merges blocked until checks pass
Fast feedback (cached deps, parallel jobs)

practices.label: Legible, attributable history
practices.what: You can see where AI helped and how it fared; automation gets reliable signals.
starter: Conventional commit format (feat/fix/chore…)
AI co-authorship attributed in commits/PRs
Small, focused PRs that are easy to review

groups.label: Documentation & Knowledge
examples: D5's signal only credits a README (1364 chars) and CONTRIBUTING.md, but commit history and code (fumadocs-based content/docs, llms.txt/llms.mdx export routes, sitemap.md, recurring 'Sync skill docs from content/docs' commits) point to a much larger structured documentation corpus than a bare README implies, so the signal likely understates documentation depth.

D5 reports 'No README detected,' which is difficult to reconcile with a 25k-star, actively maintained public monorepo that otherwise shows deep CONTRIBUTING.md, CHANGELOG, and ADR investment — this looks more like a detection miss (e.g., nonstandard path/casing or a docs-site-only front matter) than a true absence.

apps/docs ships a full fumadocs-powered documentation site (chat-sdk.dev) with guides and resources referenced from AGENTS.md, beyond the basic README/CONTRIBUTING/CHANGELOG/examples signals counted — this could push D5 above its signalScore of 55.

groups.label: CI/CD & Delivery
examples: D3 lists 'Policy-as-code (OPA/conftest)' as present, but no Rego/OPA/conftest file appears anywhere in the sampled evidence; the only related tooling visible is 'konsistent' (a custom internal structural-consistency checker referenced in package.json), which is not an OPA/conftest-based policy-as-code system, so this signal may be misattributed.

D3's signal (100, implying CI fully gates delivery) sits alongside branch-protection data showing required status checks = no, meaning the 5 CI workflows must run but are not actually enforced as a hard condition for merging.

The 'Infrastructure-as-Code present' and 'progressive delivery / feature flags' signals for D3 may be false positives: sampled files show this repo's own domain is Terraform resources for Vercel's product (e.g. client/deployment_protection_exception_test.go, a newFeatureFlagTestClient helper), not the repository's own IaC-driven or progressive-delivery deployment pipeline.

The D3 signal's "Policy-as-code (OPA/conftest)" detection is likely a mislabel of zizmor — a GitHub Actions workflow security linter run via `poe lint-zizmor` and listed as a dev dependency (`zizmor>=1.24.1`) in pyproject.toml — rather than true policy-as-code (OPA/conftest evaluating Terraform/K8s-style manifests).

groups.label: AI Tooling & Conventions
examples: A skills/ directory kept in sync from content/docs (via scripts/sync-skill-docs.sh and recurring CI commits) suggests structured agent-skill tooling exists that D1 ('Found Cursor rules' only) and D8 ('no dedicated AI process/harness... prompt library') may not be crediting, though it's ambiguous whether it serves internal dev agents or is purely an end-user product feature.

AGENTS.md is organized hierarchically (root file plus per-package files like packages/adapter-discord/AGENTS.md) and includes a published Agent Skill (.agents/skills/add-adapter) and a separate AGENTS.md shipped to SDK consumers — this multi-file, technique-rich structure suggests D1's signalScore of 50 may understate content quality relative to a typical single-file CLAUDE.md stub.

The D1 signalScore of 58 may understate agent-guidance maturity: sampled evidence shows a hierarchical system (root AGENTS.md, package-scoped packages/cli/AGENTS.md with explicit task routing, examples/nextjs/AGENTS.md, a CLAUDE.md that @-imports AGENTS.md, and a dedicated .agents/skills/cli-ux/SKILL.md library) — nested scoping, skills, and @-imports are advanced techniques the flat signal may not fully credit.

D1's high score may be partly inflated by duplication: the identical 'VERCEL BEST PRACTICES' AGENTS.md block appears verbatim in both rust/wait-until and rust/websocket (and likely other dirs), which is boilerplate propagation rather than bespoke per-example guidance, even though the root CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and starter/cms-sanity-graphql-fragments/CLAUDE.md do show genuine bespoke depth.

groups.label: Supply Chain & Security
examples: The Token permissions check states '0/1 workflows set an explicit permissions: scope,' but the sampled .github/workflows/release.yml clearly defines a job-level permissions block (contents: write, pull-requests: write, id-token: write) — the workflow does set explicit permissions, even though the grant is broad, so the '0 workflows' framing appears to misstate the evidence.

The 'signed releases' check reports 0/10 for no artifact signing/provenance, but trigger-release.yml uses OIDC trusted publishing with npm (`permissions: id-token: write`) and installs npm >=11.5.1, which since that version automatically attaches provenance attestations on publish — this may be an undercounted signal rather than a true absence of release provenance.

The sampled .github/workflows/publish.yml explicitly declares a `permissions:` block (contents: write, id-token: write, pull-requests: write), so the stated '0/1 workflows set an explicit permissions: scope' appears to undercount — the scope is explicit, just broad/non-least-privilege, which the summary should distinguish from having no permissions declaration at all.

The recent commit 'chore(deps): Bump the npm_and_yarn group across 1 directory with 3 updates (#596)' reads as a classic Dependabot grouped-update PR title, which is in tension with the D9 finding of '0/10 — No dependency-update tool committed'; a dependabot.yml may exist but wasn't in the sampled evidence.

The 'API-schema validation' signal may actually be detecting the fixture-owned 'eve eval' e2e suites (behavioral agent evals), not a dedicated schema-validation tool like Schemathesis/Dredd/Spectral — worth confirming the detector didn't conflate the two.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions

The guidance covers package-dependency graphs, per-directory purpose tables, and package-level usage docs (packages/ai/AGENTS.md) with runnable code examples, and a dedicated ADR-authoring skill built explicitly for agentic coding workflows shows the org treats agent onboarding as maintained product surface, not an afterthought.

Distinct test, test:ci, and test:update package.json scripts show the team differentiates local runs, CI-gated runs, and snapshot updates rather than treating testing as one undifferentiated suite.

dimensions.name: Commit & Velocity Signals

Much of the bot attribution traces to the changesets release bot's version-bump commits rather than LLM pair-programming co-authorship, so the 'AI-native' commit signal here is partly release-automation rather than AI-assisted authorship — still a legitimate maturity signal, but worth interpreting precisely.

70% conventional-commit compliance visible directly in the sampled commit messages (fix:, feat:, chore:)

dimensions.name: AI Process & Harness
dimensions.summary: The repo has real harness infrastructure for AI process: a dedicated ADR-authoring skill with Socratic questioning and an agent-readiness checklist explicitly designed so 'a human approves the decision; an agent implements it,' plus structured issue templates and multiple harness-* packages that formalize how different agent runtimes (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, deepagents, pi) integrate with the SDK. Combined with a protected, signed-commit branch ruleset, this is a well-above-average, repeatable structure for AI-driven contribution, though it's not fully clear from sampled evidence how much of this harness is exercised on the org's own day-to-day changes versus being product surface built for external users.

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security

report.headline: vercel/ai sits at the L3/L4 boundary: exceptional, product-grade agent guidance and one of the largest substantive test suites we've assessed carry it into Integrated territory, but the org's own PR/review loop shows almost no agentic participation and its CI security posture (a critical workflow-injection finding, no SAST, no SBOM) lags well behind its testing and documentation maturity.
strengths: Unified, deeply detailed agent guidance (AGENTS.md mirrored into CLAUDE.md, plus a .claude/ directory and package-level AGENTS.md files) gives coding agents a current architecture map and runnable examples
926 substantive test files with a 0.21 test-to-source ratio, Playwright e2e, and API-schema validation make AI-generated changes verifiable at scale
Fully automated release pipeline (changesets, 11 CI workflows) paired with a fast, small-batch commit cadence (83% small PRs, 0.3h median merge time) and 70% conventional-commit compliance

Purpose-built agent-process artifacts — an ADR-authoring skill designed for 'a human approves, an agent implements,' and multiple agent-harness packages — show the org treats agent-readiness as a maintained capability, not an afterthought
Strong release-integrity hygiene: 100% pinned Action references, signed/provenance releases, and automated dependency updates
risks: The org builds agent-harness products for others but shows 0% AI-involvement in its own 40 sampled PRs and no AI review bot — its own workflow doesn't yet dogfood the agentic review loop its products enable
A critical dangerous-workflow finding (untrusted input in a run step) plus 2 workflows with broad write permissions create a real CI injection/privilege-escalation exposure
No SAST and no SBOM generation mean first-party vulnerabilities and dependency provenance aren't systematically checked, despite the package's very wide downstream reach
Review coverage is thin relative to merge speed (25% reviewed rate, 0.3 avg reviews/PR, 0.3h median time-to-merge) — a pattern that could strain as AI-authored change volume grows
A root README was not detected by the scan; if genuinely thin or absent, it leaves a canonical entry point missing despite otherwise deep documentation

roadmap.title: Agent-assisted review is largely invisible in your own PR history, even though you build that exact capability for others
roadmap.rationale: Zero measured AI-involvement across the sampled PRs, and no AI review bot, means the trust-building work of 'AI reviews AI' hasn't been proven inside the team's own loop — a gap that matters more as the harness-* packages mature and change volume grows.
explore: What would it look like to let an agent weigh in on a sample of PRs — docs, provider boilerplate, dependency bumps — before requiring full human review?
Is there an opportunity to dogfood the harness-claude-code / harness-codex packages as part of your own review loop rather than only as product surface?
Which categories of change feel safe enough today to let an agent review first, and which still feel too risky?

roadmap.title: A critical dangerous-workflow pattern and two broad-write CI permissions sit unaddressed
roadmap.rationale: An untrusted-input-in-run-step pattern in slack-team-review-notification.yml, plus 2 workflows with broad write token scope, are exactly the low-effort, high-blast-radius issues that undermine trust in CI autonomy — especially relevant if agents start proposing workflow changes themselves.
explore: Would it help to walk through slack-team-review-notification.yml together and see exactly where untrusted input reaches the run step?
Which of the 2 broad-write workflows could be scoped down to read-only or job-specific permissions without breaking their function?
Is tightening token permissions something worth doing proactively now, before more automation gets layered on top?

roadmap.title: No static analysis or SBOM currently sits between code and release
roadmap.rationale: With no CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar wired in and no SBOM generation, first-party vulnerabilities and dependency provenance aren't systematically surfaced — a gap that compounds as more of the codebase is touched by AI-assisted changes at high velocity.
explore: Is adding a SAST pass something the team would want triggered by a specific incident, or is this more about closing a known gap proactively?
Given how widely this package is depended on downstream, has SBOM generation come up as a consumer request?
Would a lightweight first step (e.g., CodeQL on the core 'ai' and 'provider' packages only) be a reasonable place to start?

roadmap.title: Review depth looks thin relative to how fast changes merge
roadmap.rationale: A 25% reviewed-rate and 0.3 average reviews per PR, alongside a 0.3-hour median time-to-merge, suggests many changes ship with limited human scrutiny — understanding whether that reflects justified trust in tests/CI or an unintentional gap matters before AI-assisted PR volume grows further.
explore: Is the low review rate concentrated in bot-authored version-bump PRs, or does it extend into feature and provider-integration work too?
As AI-assisted contributions increase, would the team want review depth to scale with a change's risk profile rather than staying flat?
Does the 1-approval branch rule reflect the actual review bar the team wants, or has it drifted from current practice?

roadmap.title: The scan didn't find a root README — worth confirming what a first-time visitor, human or agent, actually lands on
roadmap.rationale: Even with strong CONTRIBUTING/CHANGELOG/ADR documentation, a missing or unusually thin root README would leave new contributors and coding agents cloning the repo cold without a canonical orientation point.
explore: Is the README perhaps intentionally minimal with content redirected to the docs site — and if so, is that redirect obvious to something that isn't a browser, like a cloning agent?
Would surfacing the AGENTS.md architecture table from the root README give both humans and agents a single, faster front door?

discrepancies.claim: D5 reports 'No README detected,' which is difficult to reconcile with a 25k-star, actively maintained public monorepo that otherwise shows deep CONTRIBUTING.md, CHANGELOG, and ADR investment — this looks more like a detection miss (e.g., nonstandard path/casing or a docs-site-only front matter) than a true absence.

D3 lists 'Policy-as-code (OPA/conftest)' as present, but no Rego/OPA/conftest file appears anywhere in the sampled evidence; the only related tooling visible is 'konsistent' (a custom internal structural-consistency checker referenced in package.json), which is not an OPA/conftest-based policy-as-code system, so this signal may be misattributed.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions
dimensions.summary: Root CLAUDE.md is a one-line @-import of AGENTS.md, which is itself a deep, well-organized guidance file covering concrete build/test/typecheck/release commands, a monorepo architecture map, and explicit constraints. report.headline: vercel/examples pairs unusually deep, distributed AI-agent guidance and best-in-class delivery automation with almost no AI embedded in the pipeline itself and thin CI hardening — the raw materials for high trust are there, but the loop from agent guidance to autonomous, verifiable contribution isn't closed yet.
strengths: Agent guidance is distributed, not just a single root file — dozens of individual examples carry their own AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md tailored to that example's stack
Delivery automation is exceptional for an examples monorepo: 5 CI workflows automate per-template build-and-deploy, with release automation and progressive delivery
Guardrails are enforced rather than decorative: pre-commit lint-staged, granular CODEOWNERS, and 100% PR review coverage under branch protection with signed commits
Review velocity is fast and PRs run small (median 0.3h to first review, 5.3h to merge, 45% small PRs) — infrastructure well suited to high-frequency AI-assisted contribution
risks: AI hasn't joined the pipeline itself (D4=12): no review bots, no LLM steps in CI, no auto-fix loops — all current AI benefit is individual, not systemic
CI hardening is thin (D9=48): unscoped workflow tokens, no SAST, unpinned Actions, and no signed releases/SBOM — a growing risk as more automated changes flow through this CI
Test depth may not scale with example count: 47 test files against ~190+ examples, and sampled tests look like default framework scaffolding rather than deliberate coverage
AI-attributed activity (3% of PRs, 2/30 commits) is thin relative to the investment already made in agent guidance, suggesting an adoption or attribution gap
No evals or golden-test harness exists to verify AI-authored examples are correct beyond ad hoc human PR review

roadmap.title: AI review or auto-fix hasn't yet joined the CI loop
roadmap.rationale: The review/merge loop is fully human today despite deep, per-example agent guidance already existing — wiring an AI pass into CI could compound the investment already made in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md rather than leaving it as documentation only.
explore: What would it look like to have an agent triage or pre-review new example PRs against the AGENTS.md conventions before a human looks at them?
Is there a class of PR — README fixes, lint cleanups, dependency bumps — safe enough to let an agent open or resolve autonomously?

roadmap.title: Workflow tokens run unscoped and Action references aren't pinned
roadmap.rationale: None of the 5 workflows scope `permissions:`, and none of the 13 third-party Action references are pinned by SHA — a soft target if an agent, a compromised dependency, or a mutated tag ever got a foothold in a workflow that also holds deploy tokens.
explore: What's the actual blast radius today if one of these workflows' default token were misused — could it reach other examples or the Vercel deploy tokens?
Would pinning the handful of most-used Actions by SHA be a low-effort way to raise confidence before layering more automation on top of CI?

roadmap.title: Test depth may not be keeping pace with the number of examples
roadmap.rationale: 47 test files across roughly 190+ independent example apps suggests most examples ship without dedicated tests, and the sampled tests look like default framework scaffolding rather than example-specific behavior checks — worth understanding before leaning on agents to modify examples unsupervised.
explore: Which examples are the highest-traffic templates that would benefit most from real tests if agents start touching them regularly?
Would a minimal 'does it build and boot' smoke test make sense as a baseline expectation for every example?

roadmap.title: No verifiable harness confirms AI-authored examples behave as intended
roadmap.rationale: The rich prompt/agent guidance has no evals or golden-test harness behind it, so trust in AI-produced changes currently rests entirely on human PR review rather than a repeatable, automatic check.
explore: If an agent proposed a new example end-to-end, what would 'looks right' mean in a way a script could check automatically?
Would a lightweight build-and-preview-deploy check for new or changed examples raise confidence in letting agents contribute more autonomously?

roadmap.title: AI-attributed activity is thin next to the AI guidance already invested
roadmap.rationale: Only 2 of 30 recent commits and 1 of 40 analyzed PRs show AI attribution, so the extensive AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md investment hasn't yet shown up as measurable AI-driven contribution — worth knowing whether that's an adoption gap or just missing attribution trailers.
explore: Are contributors already using Claude or Copilot day to day but simply not leaving attribution trailers, or is adoption genuinely still low?
Would surfacing AI-contribution stats internally change how teams make use of the agent guidance that already exists?

D1's high score may be partly inflated by duplication: the identical 'VERCEL BEST PRACTICES' AGENTS.md block appears verbatim in both rust/wait-until and rust/websocket (and likely other dirs), which is boilerplate propagation rather than bespoke per-example guidance, even though the root CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and starter/cms-sanity-graphql-fragments/CLAUDE.md do show genuine bespoke depth.

report.headline: Vercel's Flags SDK sits solidly in L3 Augmented: exceptional tests and CI/release automation make AI-generated code safe to merge on the engineering side, but the governance of AI's own growing role — review coverage, evals, and CI-embedded agents — hasn't caught up to its adoption.
strengths: An exceptional automated test suite (129 files, 0.44 test-to-source ratio, e2e + integration layers) paired with a 5-workflow CI pipeline that runs tests and lint on every change.
Mature, auditable release automation — Changesets-driven versioning, signed/provenance releases, and automated dependency updates — giving the org a reversible, largely hands-off path to production.

Real, if uneven, investment in agent-native tooling: per-package CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files, an @-file-reference pattern, and an emerging 'skills' system (validate-skills.mjs, skill-identifier commits).
A strong baseline review culture: 96% of merged PRs carry an approving review, and CODEOWNERS locks down security-sensitive release-workflow files to a named maintainer.
The org visibly dogfoods its own product — a feature-flag/progressive-delivery SDK — inside its own delivery pipeline.
risks: AI-involved PRs are reviewed at roughly a third the rate of the overall population (33% vs 96%) — as AI's share of contributions grows, unreviewed AI-authored changes could grow with it.

No agentic harness exists yet: no evals/golden tests for AI output, no AI code-review bot, and no LLM step inside CI — AI contributions rely on ad hoc human judgment rather than a repeatable, verifiable process.

Workflow permissions aren't scoped (0/5 workflows declare least-privilege permissions, one grants broad write) and Action pinning is nearly absent (1/31) — a single compromised tag or dependency could reach far.
Branch protection requires approvals but not passing status checks, so the well-built test/lint CI isn't actually a hard gate on merge.

Agent guidance and documentation depth vary sharply across the monorepo — rich architecture docs in vercel-flags-core, a two-line stub in playground — so an agent's effectiveness depends heavily on which package it's working in.

report.headline: Next.js runs a highly mature engineering harness — deep test coverage, technique-rich agent guidance, and a tightly gated merge process — but its automated supply-chain security controls (SAST, dependency updates, signing, SBOM) lag well behind everything else, and its own documented workflow-permission guidance isn't yet applied consistently.
strengths: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md pair delivers concrete, codebase-specific guidance (architecture map, entry points, README-reading discipline, CI-security rules) rather than a generic stub
An exceptional test suite (18,596 files, 2.98 test-to-source ratio, multi-bundler e2e matrix, a11y and API-schema checks) makes AI-generated changes genuinely verifiable before merge
Merge gates are strict and enforced: 17-rule branch protection requiring approval, code-owner review, status checks, linear history, and signed commits
Real automation is already present: an AI code-review agent in the pipeline, a bot-authored automated PR in recent history, and an eval harness (run-evals.js) for testable AI-adjacent output
Fast, small-batch delivery cadence (median 1.6h to merge, 80% small PRs) shows a well-oiled human contribution pipeline that autonomy could build on
risks: Supply-chain security posture (D9=37) is the clear outlier: no SAST, no dependency-update automation, no signing/provenance, no SBOM — a gap that matters more, not less, as more automated/AI-driven changes flow through the pipeline
A critical dangerous-workflow finding (untrusted input in a run step in build_and_test.yml) is currently unaddressed
The team's own documented least-privilege workflow-permission pattern is followed in only 3 of 11 workflows, leaving a gap between written policy and practice
The sampled CODEOWNERS file shows no actual ownership rules despite code-owner review being a required branch-protection gate, so that gate's real targeting is unclear
AI involvement in PRs is still small (3%) and too sparse to tell whether AI-touched PRs receive the same review rigor as the rest

roadmap.title: Workflow least-privilege guidance exists on paper, not fully in practice yet
roadmap.rationale: The team's own .github/AGENTS.md prescribes `permissions: {}` at the workflow level with minimal per-job grants and SHA-pinning for all actions, and pinning is followed perfectly (42/42). Yet only 3 of 11 workflows currently set an explicit permissions block, and one workflow (build_and_test.yml) has a flagged untrusted-input pattern. Given how automated the pipeline already is (36 workflows, bot-authored PRs), an over-privileged token is a real blast-radius risk if any one workflow is compromised.
explore: What would it take to bring the remaining workflows in line with the least-privilege pattern already written down in .github/AGENTS.md?
Has the untrusted-input path in build_and_test.yml come up in any recent discussion, or is it worth a closer look together?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain automation (SAST, dependency updates, signing, SBOM) hasn't caught up to the rest of the pipeline
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection, code review, and pinning discipline are all strong, but there's no SAST wired into CI, no committed dependency-update bot, no SBOM generation, and no artifact signing or provenance on releases. For a project at this scale and with this much downstream reach, these are the controls that let an org extend more trust to automated and AI-authored changes without a human re-checking every dependency and workflow by hand.
explore: Would a CodeQL or Semgrep pass alongside the existing lint/test/build stages change how confidently the team merges AI-authored diffs?
Is leaving dependency updates to manual triage a deliberate choice, or just something that hasn't been revisited recently?
What would a minimal signing/provenance story look like for canary releases, given how frequently they ship?

roadmap.title: AI involvement in PRs is small relative to the AI tooling already invested in the repo
roadmap.rationale: Only 3% of sampled PRs show AI involvement, and that sample is too small to say whether those PRs get the same review rigor as the rest. The repo already has deep AI infrastructure (AGENTS.md, .claude/, an eval harness) that appears underused relative to its depth — a gap between investment and adoption.
explore: Is the low visible AI-PR rate a sign that AI-assisted work isn't consistently attributed/tagged, or that adoption is genuinely still early?
Once there's more volume, would it be worth checking whether AI-touched PRs clear the same review bar as everything else?

roadmap.title: CODEOWNERS is wired into the merge gate but the sampled file doesn't yet define ownership
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection requires code-owner review as one of its 17 ruleset rules, but the sampled CODEOWNERS file contains only the boilerplate comment header with no path-to-owner mappings. If that's representative of the full file, the code-owner gate may be satisfied procedurally without actually routing review to the people closest to a given area of the monorepo.
explore: Does CODEOWNERS have rules further down that this sample didn't capture, or is it still close to the template?
Which parts of the monorepo — turbopack/, packages/next, docs/ — would benefit most from explicit ownership mapping if it isn't there yet?

roadmap.title: Agentic review/fix loops exist but are still narrow in scope
roadmap.rationale: There's an AI code-review agent and issue/PR automation already in the pipeline, but no visible auto-merge-on-green or dependency-update bot, and D4 sits roughly at the midpoint of the scale — notably lower than the test and CI dimensions. Deepening this loop is often what separates 'agents assist individuals' from 'agents are embedded in the process.'
explore: Is there a natural next automation to layer in alongside the existing AI reviewer — auto-merge for green, low-risk PRs, or a dependency-update bot?
Has Renovate/Dependabot-style automation been considered and set aside deliberately, or is it just not prioritized yet?

discrepancies.claim: The sampled .github/CODEOWNERS file contains only the boilerplate comment header with no actual path/owner rules, so D6's credit for a CODEOWNERS-backed code-owner review gate may overstate how substantively that gate is targeted.

The 'versioned DB migrations' signal is unusual for a frontend framework repo and most likely comes from migration files inside example apps (e.g. Prisma-based entries under examples/) rather than the core Next.js delivery pipeline having its own database migration discipline, so D3's score may be slightly inflated by this signal.

report.headline: Vercel Sandbox is an engineering-mature, fast-shipping team (98% merge rate, 1.6h median merge time, disciplined small-batch PRs) that has not yet built AI-native scaffolding — its own agent guidance, agentic review loops, AI-output harness, and supply-chain hardening all lag well behind its release velocity and human-review discipline.

roadmap.title: Agent guidance is narrow — AGENTS.md covers only the release workflow
roadmap.rationale: Agents currently have almost no documented context about how the monorepo builds, tests, or is structured beyond changeset mechanics, which limits how much unsupervised work can safely be delegated to them.
explore: What would an agent need to know about this codebase's architecture and test commands to make a safe, correct change without a human re-deriving that context each time?
Are there constraints or 'never do X' rules the team already applies informally that would be worth writing down for agents?

roadmap.title: No harness exists yet to check AI-generated output before it ships

roadmap.title: Supply-chain hardening hasn't kept pace with release velocity
roadmap.rationale: The release pipeline grants broad write/token permissions and runs unpinned third-party Actions with no SAST or dependency-update automation — a comfortable target if the team wants to extend more autonomy to agents driving CI, since agent-triggered runs would inherit the same broad blast radius.
explore: What's the smallest change that would narrow the publish workflow's token scope to only what the release step actually needs?
Would pinning the 5 Action references by SHA change how much the team trusts an agent to modify CI configuration?
Is dependency-update automation (Renovate/Dependabot) something the team has consciously deferred, or just hasn't gotten to yet?

roadmap.title: CI results inform merges but aren't a required gate
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection requires human approval and code-owner review but not passing status checks, so the safety net today is entirely human attention — a pattern that scales less well if AI-authored PR volume increases.

Would requiring the existing test/build checks to pass before merge change anything about today's workflow, or is it already de-facto enforced by reviewers?

roadmap.title: There's no AI-in-the-loop review or automation touching this repo's own process yet
roadmap.rationale: AI currently participates in this repo at a token level (one co-authored PR) rather than as part of the process itself — no review bot, no CI-embedded LLM step, no automated dependency-update merging — so the team hasn't yet tested how much it can trust an agent operating inside its own pipeline.

roadmap.title: Agent guidance is unwritten — each AI tool starts from zero context
roadmap.rationale: Without a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, every Copilot/Cursor/Claude session has to re-infer the pnpm/vitest workflow, the snapshot-update discipline, and the JSX-purity constraint from README prose — raising the odds that AI-authored changes miss constraints a shared, agent-readable file could make explicit.
explore: What would it look like to capture the workflow already documented in CONTRIBUTING.md (pnpm setup, snapshot updates, playground dev loop) into a form an agent could load automatically?
Which tribal rules — like 'JSX must be pure and stateless' or 'always update snapshots' — would most reduce risk if written down explicitly for agents?

roadmap.title: AI participation in review is more infrastructure than habit
roadmap.rationale: An AI review bot and PR automation already exist in the pipeline, but only about 5% of recent PRs show any AI involvement — the tooling is present without yet being load-bearing in the day-to-day review loop, so its potential to catch issues before the sole code owner does isn't being realized.
explore: What's keeping AI-assisted review from being the default rather than the exception on incoming PRs?
If the AI review bot flagged something today, would it get noticed, or does it need more visibility in the existing flow?

roadmap.title: There's no way yet to tell a verified AI change from an unverified one
roadmap.rationale: There's no evals/golden-test harness or prompt/agent-spec library, so as AI contribution grows there's no repeatable, inspectable process distinguishing a verified AI change from an unverified one — the branch-protection rules are strong, but weren't designed with AI-authorship specifically in mind.
explore: What would 'verified AI output' look like here, given the image-snapshot suite is already a strong behavioral oracle?
Is there an appetite for a lightweight prompts/ or agents/ folder documenting how contributors are actually using Cursor/Copilot/Claude on this repo?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain automation hasn't caught up to the release hardening already underway
roadmap.rationale: The team clearly already invests here — recent commits remove pull_request_target, declare minimal permissions, and move releases to OIDC trusted publishing — yet there's no SAST scanning, no committed Dependabot/Renovate config, and most Action refs still float on tags rather than pinned SHAs, leaving gaps in the same threat model already being actively hardened.
explore: Given the recent permission-hardening work, does extending that same instinct to dependency updates and Action pinning feel like a natural next step?
Would a lightweight CodeQL or Semgrep pass fit into the existing `pnpm ci-check` gate?

roadmap.title: Review coverage on merged PRs (32%) sits below what branch protection implies
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection requires an approval and code-owner review, yet only 32% of sampled merged PRs carry a recorded approving review — worth understanding whether this reflects small/trivial PRs, an owner self-merge path, or a reporting artifact, since it shapes how much the human safety net can be relied on as AI-authored PR volume grows.
explore: Is the 32% reviewed-rate mostly small, low-risk PRs that skip review by design, or does it reflect merges bypassing the review gate?
As AI-assisted PRs grow, would it help to track review coverage specifically for AI-authored changes?

Because this repository is entirely Speakeasy-generated (CONTRIBUTING.md explicitly tells contributors that direct pull requests are not accepted), there has been little pressure to publish agent-facing conventions, but that also means any human or AI working in this repo has no documented build/test/run commands, architecture map, or 'do not hand-edit generated code' constraint beyond what can be inferred from package.json and file headers.

dimensions.name: Automated Testing
dimensions.summary: Only 2 test files were detected, and package.json defines no "test" script at all — the workflow named "Test" (sdk_test.yaml) simply delegates to an external reusable workflow owned by speakeasy-api/sdk-generation-action, so almost none of the actual test logic or coverage practice is visible in this repository. A sampled commit — "fix: disable test/mock server generation to reduce tree size (#308)" — shows the team actively turning test/mock generation off to shrink the published package, and tsconfig excludes src/__tests__ from the build, reinforcing that the thin test footprint is a deliberate generation-pipeline choice rather than a growing suite.
strengths: A named Test workflow runs on every pull request against main
Some generated test files exist and are excluded cleanly from the shipped build
gaps: No local "test" script in package.json
Test/mock generation was deliberately disabled to reduce package size, shrinking coverage

dimensions.name: CI/CD & Delivery
dimensions.summary: CI is genuinely multi-stage: 3 GitHub Actions workflows cover pull-request testing, a nightly (cron) SDK regeneration job, and automated publishing — a real, largely hands-off delivery pipeline for a generated client. However, the detected "progressive delivery / feature flags" signal looks like a likely false positive: the sampled evidence (commit messages referencing `vercel.featureFlags.deleteFlagSegment()`, docs modeling Vercel's Feature Flags product) shows the SDK merely wraps Vercel's own Feature Flags API as a resource, not that vercel/sdk's own pipeline ships changes behind feature flags. Both core workflows also mostly wrap an external reusable workflow (speakeasy-api/sdk-generation-action@v15), so the actual lint/test/build/publish steps are opaque to this repo.
strengths: 3 workflows covering test, scheduled generation, and publish
Nightly cron-triggered regeneration keeps the SDK in sync with the upstream API automatically
Automated publish step reduces manual release toil
Branch protection gates what can land on main
gaps: Core pipeline logic is delegated to an opaque third-party reusable workflow
The 'progressive delivery / feature flags' signal is likely a misattribution of the SDK's own feature-flags API coverage
No visible IaC, GitOps, or declarative infra-as-code in the sample
No required CI status checks configured in the branch ruleset to make the pipeline actually gate merges

report.headline: vercel/sdk runs a genuinely automated, scheduled code-generation and release pipeline with strict branch protection, but almost none of the hallmark AI-native *development* practices are present — no agent guidance, no AI-assisted review, a deliberately thinned test suite, and no supply-chain hardening — putting the org at L2 Assisted, propped up mainly by generation-bot cadence rather than a team AI workflow.
strengths: A scheduled (nightly), fully automated SDK regeneration and publish pipeline keeps the client in sync with the upstream API with minimal human toil
Branch protection is genuinely strict: signed commits, required code-owner review, linear history, 7 ruleset rules
TypeScript strictest configuration plus a zero-warnings linter (oxlint) enforced on every change
Zero known vulnerabilities across dependencies and a clear SECURITY.md disclosure path
Extensive generated documentation surface (README, per-model docs, runnable examples) usable by both humans and agents
risks: No shared agent/AI guidance (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) exists, so any AI assistance applied to this repo is ad hoc and could conflict with what the nightly generator will overwrite
Test/mock generation was deliberately disabled to reduce package size, leaving generated breaking changes largely unverified before publish
Supply-chain hardening (SAST, pinned Actions, dependency-update automation, signing, SBOM) is essentially absent despite privileged, unattended automation running nightly with write access

The headline 97% 'AI-attributed' commit figure is mostly templated generation-bot output rather than genuine AI-assisted engineering, which could overstate this org's actual AI-native workflow maturity if read at face value
CONTRIBUTING.md forecloses the PR-based contribution loop entirely, limiting how generator bugs or doc gaps get fixed and reviewed

roadmap.title: Agents (and new contributors) have no shared map of this repo to work from
roadmap.rationale: Without something like an AGENTS.md describing the generation pipeline, build commands, and the 'this code is regenerated nightly, don't hand-edit it' constraint, any AI assistant invoked here risks proposing edits that get silently clobbered on the next regeneration cycle.
explore: What would an agent need to know before touching this repo — that the code is generated, that direct PRs aren't accepted, that regeneration runs nightly?
Would a short, agent-readable note pointing to the real spec source save contributors from wasted edits?

roadmap.title: Test generation was intentionally turned off, so the safety net is thinner than the pipeline suggests
roadmap.rationale: A sampled commit shows test/mock generation being disabled to shrink package size — reasonable for shipping size, but it also means very little automated verification stands between a spec change and a published SDK version.
explore: Now that tree-size pressure pushed tests out of the shipped package, could tests still run in CI without being bundled into the published artifact?
What would give the team confidence that a generated breaking change is intentional rather than a generator bug?

roadmap.title: Review and merge still rely entirely on human judgment, with no AI-assisted check on the generator's own output
roadmap.rationale: Since generated PRs land automatically from upstream spec diffs, a lightweight AI reviewer skimming those diffs for anomalies (unexpected breaking changes, malformed types) could catch generator mistakes before they reach npm.
explore: Given how much of this repo's change volume is machine-generated, is there value in an AI reviewer double-checking the generator's own output before merge?
What would it take to try an AI review pass on just the nightly generation PRs first, as a low-risk pilot?

roadmap.title: Actions and dependencies aren't pinned or scanned, despite a nightly pipeline that runs with write access
roadmap.rationale: The generation and publish workflows carry contents:write and id-token:write permissions; unpinned third-party Actions and the absence of SAST or dependency-update automation is exactly the kind of gap that turns a convenient automation into a supply-chain exposure.
explore: Would pinning the 3 external Action references to SHAs change how much confidence the team has in the nightly pipeline?
Is there appetite for turning on CodeQL or a dependency-update tool, given how much unattended write-access automation already runs?

roadmap.title: The contribution loop is closed to outside changes, which also closes off a feedback path for agents
roadmap.rationale: CONTRIBUTING.md tells everyone — human or AI — that PRs aren't accepted here, which is reasonable for generated code but leaves no structured, agent-usable path for reporting or fixing generator-level bugs; everything funnels into an issue tracker with no visible triage SLA or Definition-of-Done.
explore: Is there an upstream spec or generator repo where an AI agent could actually act on issues raised against this SDK?
Would linking CONTRIBUTING.md to that upstream repo give agents and humans a real path to fix root causes instead of just filing issues here?

discrepancies.claim: The 'progressive delivery / feature flags' signal is likely a false positive — sampled evidence (commit messages referencing `vercel.featureFlags.deleteFlagSegment()`, docs modeling Vercel's Feature Flags API) shows this is the SDK's coverage of Vercel's Feature Flags product, not the repo's own delivery pipeline using feature-flag-gated rollouts.

signalScore=20 may still overstate active testing rigor — commit #308 ('disable test/mock server generation to reduce tree size') and the tsconfig exclusion of src/__tests__ suggest the 2 detected test files are vestigial artifacts rather than a maintained, growing suite.

The 97% AI/bot-attributed commit figure conflates a deterministic Speakeasy code-generation bot with genuine AI-assisted development; only one sampled commit shows an actual LLM co-author trailer ('Co-authored-by: Claude Sonnet 4.6'), so the high score reflects automation cadence more than human-AI collaboration depth.

report.headline: Vercel Shop lives an AI-native day-to-day workflow — heavy AI-authored commit history and unusually rich, multi-file agent guidance — but the verification harness around it (testing, review gating, CI-status enforcement) hasn't caught up to the pace, so a meaningful share of AI-driven changes ship with little to check them.
strengths: Deep, layered AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md guidance scoped per app, with explicit 'MUST' rules and a custom skills/plugin system agents can install and invoke via slash commands
Commit history strongly corroborates an AI-native workflow: 80% AI/bot-attributed commits, 97% conventional-commit style, 28% of PRs involve Claude, active daily cadence
Release automation is mature and secure: changesets versioning, GitHub-API commit signing, and npm Trusted Publisher OIDC provenance form a genuinely auditable path to production
Branch protection is strict for a repo this size: required approval, code-owner review, signed commits, and linear history enforced via 9 ruleset rules
risks: AI-authored work is essentially unreviewed at merge time: 0% of AI-involved PRs carry an approving review, overall PR review coverage is 6%, and median time-to-merge is 0.5h
Automated test coverage is minimal — a single test file scoped to the CLI scaffolding tool — leaving the core storefront template and docs app without regression protection for AI-authored changes
No agentic verification loop exists yet: no AI review bot, no LLM-in-CI step, no auto-fix/auto-merge or dependency-update automation, so authorship speed isn't matched by automated checking
Branch protection requires approvals but not passing status checks, so CI results don't actually gate what reaches main

Supply-chain hardening is uneven: CI workflow permissions are broad rather than least-privilege, most actions are unpinned, and no SAST or dependency-scanning automation runs, despite a strong release-signing story

roadmap.title: The release pipeline trusts itself with more access than it scopes out loud
roadmap.rationale: The one workflow examined grants broad write permissions and only 1 of 4 action references are pinned by SHA — this widens the blast radius if a workflow or third-party action is ever compromised, which matters more once agents are the ones touching CI and dependency configs.
explore: Would scoping this workflow's permissions down to exactly what the release job needs change the risk calculus here?
Given the trusted-publisher setup already in place, is pinning the remaining actions to SHAs a natural next step or blocked by something?

roadmap.title: AI-authored PRs move fast with no reviewer in the loop
roadmap.rationale: 28% of PRs involve AI, yet 0% of those carry an approving review, and overall review coverage sits at 6% with a 0.5h median time-to-merge — the required-approval rule exists on paper but isn't being exercised in practice for AI-assisted work.
explore: What would it take for the existing 1-approval / code-owner rule to actually apply to AI-assisted PRs before they merge?
Is the fast merge cadence here a deliberate trust decision, or has review just not kept pace with how much AI is authoring?

roadmap.title: The product's core apps carry almost no automated tests
roadmap.rationale: Only one test file exists in the whole monorepo, covering the CLI scaffolding tool — the Next.js storefront template and docs app have no visible automated tests, so there's little signal to tell an agent (or a human) whether a change actually works before it ships.
explore: Where would tests give the fastest feedback on AI-authored changes — cart/checkout logic, the Shopify GraphQL layer, locale handling?
What's made testing apps/template and apps/docs harder to prioritize than the CLI so far?

roadmap.title: CI runs, but a red pipeline doesn't stop a merge
roadmap.rationale: GitHub Actions CI is present and release automation is mature, but branch protection requires approvals and signed commits without requiring passing status checks — so the pipeline's output is informational rather than a gate, which matters more as AI authors a growing share of changes.
explore: Would requiring the existing CI checks to pass before merge change how confidently the team could lean on AI-authored PRs?
Is there a known reason status checks aren't required yet — flakiness, incomplete coverage, something else worth surfacing first?

roadmap.title: Nothing in the pipeline automatically reviews, fixes, or triages AI-driven changes
roadmap.rationale: Despite heavy day-to-day AI authorship (80% of commits, 28% of PRs), no AI review bot, LLM-in-CI step, or Renovate/Dependabot auto-merge automation was found — the loop currently stops at generation rather than closing with an automated check.
explore: What would an automated first-pass reviewer catch here that human review is currently the only thing catching?
Given the skills/plugin system already structures how agents make changes, is there an opening to structure how those changes get verified too?

discrepancies.claim: The Token permissions check states '0/1 workflows set an explicit permissions: scope,' but the sampled .github/workflows/release.yml clearly defines a job-level permissions block (contents: write, pull-requests: write, id-token: write) — the workflow does set explicit permissions, even though the grant is broad, so the '0 workflows' framing appears to misstate the evidence.

D6 reports 'no linting/typing/guardrail config detected,' but the sampled root package.json defines 'lint': 'turbo run lint' and 'format': 'turbo run format' scripts orchestrated across every app in the monorepo via Turborepo, indicating guardrail tooling is wired in even if the per-app config files themselves weren't sampled.

D5's score reflects only a short README and a changelog, but the repo contains a full documentation application (apps/docs, the vercel.shop docs site) with its own AGENTS.md and architecture — this substantial docs infrastructure doesn't appear to be credited in the signal.

posture.label: Solid but Manual

dimensions.name: Automated Testing
dimensions.summary: Testing is a clear organizational strength: 137 test files, a configured framework plus Playwright e2e, coverage tracking, and a 1.02 test-to-source ratio. The sampled e2e specs aren't smoke tests — they cover genuine, hard-won edge cases (React 19 concurrent-transition pausing, suspense retry/preload, RSC serialization, a double-unsubscribe regression guard), and CI runs the suite against both a nightly React canary build and legacy React 17, showing a deliberate cross-version compatibility philosophy.
strengths: 137 test files with a 1.02 test-to-source ratio and coverage tracking configured
Playwright e2e suite exercising real concurrency/suspense edge cases, not just happy paths
Scheduled testing against React canary and legacy React 17 in dedicated CI workflows
Regression tests tied to specific fixed issues (e.g. double-unsubscribe cache bug, issue-2702 hook overflow)
gaps: No mutation testing (Stryker/mutmut) evidenced to validate test effectiveness
No contract or API-schema testing evidenced (less relevant for a client library)
No performance/load smoke testing (k6/Lighthouse CI) evidenced
Coverage is tracked but enforcement via a merge-blocking threshold isn't confirmed

dimensions.name: CI/CD & Delivery
dimensions.summary: CI is solid and multi-layered: five workflows gate lint, test, build, and e2e, with dedicated jobs for React canary (scheduled nightly) and React 17 legacy compatibility, plus a modern release pipeline using OIDC trusted npm publishing (no long-lived publish tokens). As a published library rather than a deployed service, there's no IaC/GitOps/progressive-delivery surface to expect, but the release path itself is auditable and reasonably safe for an agent to drive.
strengths: Five CI workflows covering lint, build, unit tests, and containerized Playwright e2e
OIDC trusted npm publishing removes static publish secrets from the release path
Scheduled/matrix compatibility testing against React canary and React 17
e2e job uploads Playwright reports as artifacts for post-run inspection
gaps: Branch protection doesn't appear to require passing status checks before merge, so CI gates review but not the merge button itself
No IaC, policy-as-code, or GitOps manifests (expected for a client library, but limits 'delivery-as-code' maturity)
No semantic-release/changesets automation visible — version bumps look like manual commits (e.g. '2.4.2 (#4279)')
No progressive-delivery or feature-flag tooling (not obviously applicable to this package, but caps the ceiling)

dimensions.name: Agentic Workflows
dimensions.summary: No agentic workflows were found in any sampled CI configuration — no AI review bot, no LLM step inside a workflow, no auto-fix/auto-PR bot, and no auto-merge automation. The pipeline is entirely human-reviewed and human-triggered aside from the standard checkout/build/test steps.
evidence: No agentic/AI-in-CI workflows detected (e.g. AI review bots, LLM steps in CI, auto-merge)
gaps: No AI code-review bot (CodeRabbit, Claude/Copilot review, Greptile) wired into PRs
No LLM invocation steps inside any CI workflow
No auto-fix or auto-formatting bot loop
No Renovate/Dependabot auto-merge or issue-to-PR automation

dimensions.name: Documentation & Knowledge
dimensions.summary: Baseline documentation is reasonable — a substantial multi-section README, a CONTRIBUTING.md, and an examples directory — but from the sampled evidence deeper knowledge infrastructure is thin: no ADRs, no in-repo CHANGELOG.md was surfaced, and the canonical API documentation lives off-repo on swr.vercel.app rather than as agent-readable in-repo docs.
strengths: Substantial README (3737 chars, 4 sections) covering intro, features, and quick start
CONTRIBUTING.md present for contributor onboarding
Dedicated examples directory demonstrating real usage patterns
Canonical documentation site (swr.vercel.app) linked for deeper reference
gaps: No ADRs or decision records (docs/adr, decisions/) detected
No in-repo CHANGELOG.md surfaced despite an active release cadence
No in-repo API reference (OpenAPI/typedoc equivalent) — relies entirely on an external site
No architecture map for contributors or agents to orient quickly

dimensions.name: Code Quality & Guardrails
dimensions.summary: Guardrails are enforced, not merely present: TypeScript strict mode is confirmed in tsconfig.json, the project recently modernized its lint/format tooling (oxlint/oxfmt per commit history), CODEOWNERS is configured, and the default branch requires a code-owner-reviewed, signed-commit PR to merge — a real merge-time gate rather than a checked-in config nobody enforces.
evidence: PR review coverage 71% (14 merged · 75% small · 0% reverted)
Pull requests required to merge (1 approval(s) + code owners)
strengths: TypeScript strict mode plus additional strictness flags (noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters, strictBindCallApply)
Recently modernized formatter/linter (oxfmt/oxlint) shows active investment in guardrails
CODEOWNERS with required code-owner review and signed commits enforced at the branch-protection level
71% PR review coverage with 75% small-batch PRs supports reviewable, low-risk changes
gaps: Branch protection requires approvals but not passing status checks, per the process signals
No commitlint/conventional-commit enforcement evidenced despite 63% adoption in practice
No PR template confirmed in the sampled signals
Pre-commit hook configuration wasn't directly observed in sampled files (only inferred from signal)

dimensions.name: Commit & Velocity Signals
dimensions.summary: Commit history reflects an active, disciplined project: conventional-commit prefixes in roughly two-thirds of recent commits, a fast median time-to-merge (~20.8h) and time-to-first-review (~19.5h), 75% small PRs, and continuous activity within the last 30 days. One of the last 30 commits is co-authored by an AI agent (Cursor), but that remains an isolated instance rather than a systemic pattern.
strengths: Active, continuous commit cadence with a push within the last 30 days
63% conventional-commit style adoption in recent history
Fast median merge and first-review turnaround (under one day)
Direct evidence of a merged, AI-agent-co-authored commit (Cursor Agent)
gaps: Only 1 of 30 recent commits shows AI attribution — individual, not team-wide, usage
Measured AI-involved PR rate is 0% in the analyzed sample
No bot-authored commits (dependency bots, auto-formatters) observed in recent history

dimensions.name: AI Process & Harness
dimensions.summary: The AI-specific harness is minimal: structured issue templates and strong branch protection (signed commits, code-owner review) exist as generic contribution scaffolding, but there is no evals/golden-test layer for AI or LLM output, no prompt or agent-spec library, and no agent-oriented runbooks or Definition-of-Done — meaning any AI-authored change is verified only by the same general test suite as human-authored code, with no repeatable AI-specific harness.
strengths: Structured issue templates provide some intake discipline
Signed-commit and code-owner-review requirements act as a review gate on any change, AI-authored or not
CONTRIBUTING.md (per D5) gives at least a human-oriented contribution process to build an agent-facing one from
gaps: No evals or golden-test harness (promptfoo, evals/, golden/) for AI/LLM output
No structured prompt or agent-spec library (prompts/, .claude/agents/)
No agent-readable operational runbooks or ADRs
No explicit Definition-of-Done or review checklist tailored to AI-generated changes

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security
dimensions.summary: Security posture is fixed by the deterministic battery at 40/100 (posture 40/100; exposure unknown — no lockfile/alert access). The strong points are real: branch protection is solid (protected, 1 approval, code-owner review, signed commits) and a SECURITY.md documents a vulnerability-reporting path, with no dangerous-workflow script-injection patterns detected. But supply-chain automation is largely absent — no SAST wired into CI, no committed dependency-update tool, zero of eight Action references pinned by SHA/digest (only version tags), and no SBOM generation or artifact-signing/provenance step, despite the release pipeline's otherwise-modern OIDC trusted-publishing setup.
evidence: Branch protection [posture/high]: 8/10 — Default branch: protected, 1 approval(s), code-owner review, signed commits.
Dangerous workflow [posture/critical]: 10/10 — No script-injection or untrusted-checkout patterns detected.
Token permissions [posture/high]: 2/10 — 1/5 workflows set an explicit `permissions:` scope.
SAST [posture/medium]: 0/10 — No SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar) wired into CI.
Dependency updates [posture/high]: 0/10 — No dependency-update tool committed.
Pinned dependencies [posture/medium]: 0/10 — 0/8 Actions/images pinned by SHA/digest (8 action refs).
Security policy [posture/medium]: 10/10 — SECURITY.md documents a vulnerability-reporting path.
Signed releases [posture/high]: 0/10 — No artifact signing / provenance in CI.
Known vulnerabilities [exposure/high]: n/a/10 — Dependency vulnerabilities not inspected (no lockfile / no alert access).
strengths: Branch protection scored 8/10: protected default branch, required approval, code-owner review, signed commits
Dangerous-workflow check scored 10/10 — no script-injection or untrusted-checkout patterns
SECURITY.md present and scored 10/10 for documenting a vulnerability-reporting path
OIDC trusted npm publishing eliminates static publish tokens from the release workflow
gaps: Add CodeQL (or Semgrep) scanning that runs on pull_request.
Add a `.github/dependabot.yml` (or Renovate) config.
Pin third-party Actions to a full commit SHA (and container images to a digest).
Sign releases with cosign and emit SLSA provenance (actions/attest).
Generate an SBOM (Syft/CycloneDX) on release.
Add a least-privilege top-level `permissions:` block (default `contents: read`) to every workflow.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions
dimensions.summary: No machine-readable agent guidance (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, MCP config, prompt library) was found anywhere in the sampled repository. The only trace of AI-assisted development is a single commit co-authored by 'Cursor Agent' (#4258, pinning pnpm version) — evidence of an individual using an AI coding tool, not of a documented, shared convention an agent could pick up and follow.
evidence: No machine-readable AI/agent guidance detected (e.g. CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules)
strengths: At least one contributor is actively using an AI coding agent (Cursor) day-to-day, shown by a merged co-authored commit
gaps: No CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md or equivalent agent-facing brief exists
No documented build/test/run commands or architecture map targeted at agents
No explicit 'never/always' constraints or tool-permission policy for AI contributors
No MCP config, subagent, or slash-command setup evidenced

report.headline: vercel/swr runs a mature, rigorously-tested open-source engineering operation — deep test coverage, enforced type/lint guardrails, and a secretless OIDC release pipeline — but almost none of that maturity has yet become AI-native: there is no shared agent guidance, no agentic review or CI steps, and only one incidental AI-co-authored commit in recent history.
strengths: Exceptional automated test coverage (137 files, 1.02 test-to-source ratio) including genuine React-concurrency and suspense edge-case e2e tests, run against both React canary and legacy React 17 in CI
Enforced guardrails: TypeScript strict mode, recently modernized lint/format tooling, CODEOWNERS, and required code-owner review with signed commits on the protected default branch
Modern, secretless release pipeline via OIDC trusted npm publishing
Healthy delivery velocity: ~20h median merge/review turnaround and 75% small, mostly conventional-commit-styled PRs
risks: No machine-readable AI/agent guidance exists anywhere in the repo, so any AI contribution today starts from zero shared context rather than a documented team convention
No agentic workflows are wired into CI or review — no AI review bot, no LLM-in-CI step — so despite strong CI gates there's no compounding automation loop
Supply-chain hardening lags the rest of the pipeline: no SAST, no committed dependency-update bot, Actions pinned only to mutable version tags, and no SBOM or signed-provenance step
Branch protection requires review approval but doesn't appear to require passing status checks, leaving a gap between what CI verifies and what merge actually enforces
AI usage in the workflow is measured at a single co-authored commit out of the last 30 and 0% of analyzed PRs — any AI adoption so far is individual, not systemic

roadmap.title: Agent guidance is essentially absent — agents have no shared brief to work from
roadmap.rationale: Without a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, each contributor or agent has to rediscover build/test commands, architecture, and conventions from scratch every time, which keeps AI-assisted work individual and inconsistent instead of compounding into a shared team capability.
explore: What would it take to write down the commands and constraints an agent already has to infer today from tsconfig, package.json, and CONTRIBUTING.md?
Where do new human contributors currently learn the architecture and 'never/always' rules — could that same material be made agent-readable?
Has anyone tried pointing an agent at this repo cold? What did it get wrong that a short brief could have prevented?

roadmap.title: AI involvement in review and CI is not yet systematic — merges rely entirely on human judgment
roadmap.rationale: The existing CI gates (lint, test, build, e2e) are solid, which is exactly the foundation an AI review or triage step could build on — but right now nothing autonomous participates in the merge loop, so review quality and speed are capped by human bandwidth alone.
explore: Would an AI review pass running alongside the required human approval change reviewer confidence or workload on this repo's PR volume?
Are there recurring PR feedback patterns (style, missing tests, edge cases) that a bot could flag before a human looks?
What would need to be true for the team to trust an automated first-pass review on a library this widely depended upon?

roadmap.title: There's no repeatable harness for verifying AI-authored changes beyond the general test suite
roadmap.rationale: The test suite verifies application behavior extremely well, but there's no evals/golden-output layer or prompt/agent-spec library, so an AI-authored change is trusted only as far as the general suite covers it — there's no reusable, repeatable way to verify or replay AI-specific work.
explore: When an AI agent proposes a change today, what gives the team confidence beyond 'CI passed'?
Would a small library of proven prompts or agent configs for recurring tasks (adding a hook, writing an e2e test) save rediscovery effort?
Is there a recurring class of AI-produced mistake that a lightweight golden-test check could catch early?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain automation hasn't caught up to the release pipeline's other strengths
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection and OIDC-based npm publishing show real supply-chain thinking, but with no SAST, no committed dependency-update bot, unpinned Action refs, and no SBOM/signing step, a compromised dependency or workflow edit could slip through without any automated check noticing — a gap that matters more, not less, as more autonomous change-making enters the pipeline.
explore: Given how much of CI is already automated, what would it take to pin Actions to a SHA and add a dependency-update bot?
Is there appetite for wiring a SAST pass into the existing test workflow, given the codebase's size and dependency surface?
Now that publishing already uses OIDC trusted publishing, is there a natural next step toward attested/signed release provenance?

roadmap.title: Branch protection requires review but doesn't appear to require passing status checks
roadmap.rationale: Requiring an approval and code-owner sign-off is strong, but if the ruleset doesn't also require the Test/E2E workflows to pass, there's a theoretical path for a reviewed PR to merge despite a red build — a gap between what CI verifies and what the merge button actually enforces.
explore: Would marking the Test and E2E workflows as required status checks close a gap between verification and enforcement here?
Has a PR ever merged with a known-failing check, and was that a deliberate call or an oversight?

discrepancies.claim: The 'signed releases' check reports 0/10 for no artifact signing/provenance, but trigger-release.yml uses OIDC trusted publishing with npm (`permissions: id-token: write`) and installs npm >=11.5.1, which since that version automatically attaches provenance attestations on publish — this may be an undercounted signal rather than a true absence of release provenance.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions

This is actionable guidance an agent could actually follow, but it doesn't reach into advanced technique territory — no MCP servers, subagents, hooks, slash commands, skills, or a tool-permission policy, and no complementary CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules for other tool ecosystems.

Single guidance file only — no CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules/copilot-instructions for other assistants

dimensions.name: Automated Testing
dimensions.summary: Testing is a clear strength: 104 test files against source with a high 0.67 test-to-source ratio, a configured framework (Go testing plus terraform-plugin-testing for acceptance tests), and sampled files show substantive, behavior-level assertions rather than trivial smoke checks — retry-until-success upload logic, environment-variable conflict matching, and backward/forward-compatible API response parsing.

report.headline: Vercel's Terraform provider shows the guardrails of an L3 Augmented shop — a specific, technique-grounded AGENTS.md, deep test coverage, and strict branch/review discipline — but AI participation is still individually driven rather than embedded into automated review, fix, or supply-chain-hardening loops.
strengths: AGENTS.md gives agents real, bug-derived constraints (write-only env vars, struct-reuse pitfalls) alongside build/test/lint commands, not just a token stub
A deep, layered test suite (104 files, 0.67 test-to-source ratio) with substantive edge-case assertions gives real confidence to merge AI-generated changes
Branch protection and review discipline are strict and actually followed: required approval + code-owner review + signed commits, with 90% of merged PRs carrying an approving review
Documentation is complete and consistently structured across every resource and data source, useful to both new developers and agents
CI enforces lint and test on every change with a healthy, fast merge cadence (22.3h median)
risks: No harness verifies AI-authored output before it reaches human review — no evals, golden tests, or prompt/agent library beyond the single AGENTS.md
Supply-chain hardening is largely absent: no SAST, no dependency-update automation, no pinned action SHAs, no signing, no SBOM
Agentic workflows barely extend past a single review bot — no auto-fix, auto-PR, or LLM-driven CI steps, so AI never acts autonomously in the pipeline
AI's footprint in shipped history is thin (3% of PRs, 2 of 30 commits), suggesting adoption is still occasional and individual rather than a team norm
CI workflows carry no explicit least-privilege permissions scoping, widening blast radius if any workflow or action were compromised

roadmap.title: Agent guidance exists, but AI's presence in the CI/PR loop is still thin
roadmap.rationale: AGENTS.md gives an agent good instructions to follow, but there's no evidence yet of agents actually driving PRs, auto-fixes, or CI steps beyond a single review bot — the loop from 'agent proposes' to 'system verifies and ships' isn't wired up, so AI's contribution stays capped at individual assistance.
explore: What would it look like to let an agent open a draft PR for a small, well-scoped change (like a deprecation) and see how the existing review process holds up?
Given the acceptance-test coverage already in place, which recent PRs could plausibly have been drafted end-to-end by an agent?

roadmap.title: There's no repeatable harness that verifies AI-authored contributions before they land
roadmap.rationale: Beyond issue templates and branch protection, there's no evals/golden-test suite or prompt/agent library — so there's no inspectable, repeatable process for knowing whether an AI-suggested change meets the bar before a human reviews it.
explore: Would a small set of golden acceptance-test scenarios that any AI-suggested resource change must pass change how confident the team feels merging that code?
Is there appetite to track which PRs originate from an agent, to build a visible track record over time?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain hardening (SAST, dependency automation, pinned actions, signing) is largely absent
roadmap.rationale: With SAST, dependency-update automation, SHA-pinned actions, and release signing all at 0/10, a compromised dependency or Action would have an easier path into a provider that many teams use to manage real infrastructure.
explore: How would the team feel about a dependency-update bot opening PRs automatically, given the healthy 62% merge rate and review cadence already in place?
Is there a specific reason action refs aren't pinned by SHA yet, or has it just not come up?

roadmap.title: CI workflows run without explicit least-privilege token scoping
roadmap.rationale: Neither of the two workflows declares an explicit `permissions:` block, so jobs default to broader GITHUB_TOKEN scope than they likely need — a small config change with an outsized blast-radius reduction if a workflow or action were ever compromised.
explore: Would it be worth auditing what each workflow actually needs (read vs. write) and scoping permissions down explicitly?
Are there any workflows that currently rely on broader-than-needed token access for convenience?

roadmap.title: AI participation in shipped work looks occasional rather than habitual
roadmap.rationale: Only 2 of the last 30 commits and about 3% of PRs show AI attribution — a useful signal that AI-assisted development today is individual and experimental rather than a systemic, team-wide practice reflected in the commit trail.
explore: Among engineers already using AGENTS.md-guided assistants locally, what's stopping that work from showing up as Co-Authored-By trailers or bot commits?
Would a lightweight adoption metric (AI-assisted PRs over time) help the team see whether usage is growing?

discrepancies.claim: The 'Infrastructure-as-Code present' and 'progressive delivery / feature flags' signals for D3 may be false positives: sampled files show this repo's own domain is Terraform resources for Vercel's product (e.g. client/deployment_protection_exception_test.go, a newFeatureFlagTestClient helper), not the repository's own IaC-driven or progressive-delivery deployment pipeline.

D6's signal list omits any 'linter/formatter present' bullet, yet AGENTS.md documents an enforced stack (staticcheck, tfproviderlint, gofmt, go vet run via `task lint`) and D3 independently confirms 'CI runs linting' — this looks like a detector miss on an existing, CI-enforced guardrail.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions
dimensions.summary: Turborepo publishes both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md at the repo root, plus nested AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files inside apps/agents and example apps that use @-file-reference imports (apps/agents/CLAUDE.md is literally `@AGENTS.md`). The root AGENTS.md carries genuine technique-rich guidance rather than a stub: an architecture-map pointer (ARCHITECTURE.md), a checklist of docs to update on drift, PR-title/conventional-commit enforcement, and a strict always/never policy (no `--no-verify`, Clippy-denied `.unwrap()`/`.expect()`). What's missing is breadth: no sampled MCP server config, slash-command, or hook definitions, and the example-app AGENTS.md files are thin one-liners.

report.headline: Turborepo pairs a strong, enforced engineering core — deep behavioral tests, mature gated CI, strict Rust guardrails — with real but siloed AI-agent investment (a custom eve framework, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) that hasn't yet closed the loop into visible, governed AI-driven PRs, CI automation, or measured verification.

Genuine agent guidance (root AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md with explicit never/always rules) plus a custom-built "eve" agent framework already wired to GitHub and Slack
Strict, enforced code-quality tooling (oxlint/oxfmt, TS strict, Clippy deny unwrap/expect, pre-commit hooks) keeps a large multi-language monorepo consistent
Strong release supply-chain hygiene: signed/provenance releases, SHA-pinned Actions, and a published SECURITY.md
Fast, small-batch delivery cadence (median 4.5h merge, 57% small PRs, 93% conventional commits) that could support higher AI-driven throughput once trust catches up
risks: Two CI workflows process untrusted input in run steps — a critical-severity risk that would be amplified if agents start opening more of the PR volume
No SAST or automated dependency-update tooling means neither human- nor AI-authored code gets systematic vulnerability or staleness screening
Branch protection requires 0 approvals and doesn't enforce CODEOWNERS review, so the safety net for AI-generated changes is CI checks alone, not human sign-off
The eve agent framework and AI conventions exist, but AI involvement in the visible PR trail measures 0% — making it hard to know how agent-authored changes are actually verified before merge
No evals or golden tests were found for the eve agent's own output, so there's no measured harness for trusting what it produces

roadmap.title: Real agent infrastructure exists, but it's not yet visible in how PRs get reviewed or merged
roadmap.rationale: The team has built genuine agentic infrastructure (the eve framework, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, an ai-agents crate) but none of it currently shows up as AI review bots, LLM-in-CI steps, or measurable AI-authored PRs (0% in the sample). Until that loop closes, the investment in agent tooling stays siloed rather than compounding into faster, safer delivery.
explore: What would it take for the eve agent to participate visibly in PR review or triage?
Is there a reason AI-authored changes aren't yet flowing through the standard PR trail?
