roadmap.title: A couple of CI workflows handle untrusted input in ways that haven't been hardened
roadmap.rationale: test-js-packages.yml and turborepo-test.yml were flagged for processing untrusted input directly in run steps — a well-known script-injection risk pattern in GitHub Actions. This matters independently of AI, but becomes more pressing as more automated (including agent-driven) changes move through CI, since a compromised workflow could act as a foothold.
explore: Has the team looked at whether those two workflows need direct access to untrusted input, or whether it could go through a safer intermediate step?
Would restructuring those triggers or sandboxing the input change the risk profile meaningfully?

roadmap.title: Static analysis and dependency freshness aren't automated yet
roadmap.rationale: No SAST tool (CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar) or dependency-update bot (Dependabot/Renovate) is wired in, despite otherwise strong supply-chain hygiene elsewhere (signed releases, pinned Actions, SECURITY.md). Without these, neither human nor AI-generated code gets systematic vulnerability or staleness screening before merge.
explore: What's stopped the team from adding a SAST scan or dependency-update tool so far — tooling fit, noise, or just not prioritized yet?
Would automatic dependency PRs change how confidently the team could let an agent handle routine upgrades?

roadmap.title: CODEOWNERS defines ownership, but merges don't currently require a review from anyone
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection requires 0 approvals and doesn't enforce code-owner review, so CODEOWNERS currently documents intent without gating merges. As AI-authored changes become a larger share of contributions, human review becomes one of the few remaining checks beyond automated tests — worth knowing whether the current setting is a deliberate speed trade-off.
explore: Was the 0-required-approvals setting a deliberate trade-off for merge speed, or more that it hasn't been revisited recently?
Would a lightweight required-review rule change how comfortable the team feels merging AI-touched PRs?

roadmap.title: The eve agent's own output doesn't appear to have a measured verification harness
roadmap.rationale: A structured prompt/agent library and AI-aware contribution docs exist, but there's no sign of evals or golden tests for what the eve agent itself produces. Without that, trust in agent output relies on ad hoc human review rather than a repeatable, measurable check — a gap that matters more as the agent's scope grows.
explore: How does the team currently know when the eve agent's suggestions are good enough to act on?
Would a small set of golden-test cases for the agent's most common tasks be useful groundwork?

discrepancies.claim: D4 reports 0 agentic workflows, but apps/agents/agent/agent.ts configures a deployed AI agent (model: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8) with a GitHub channel (apps/agents/agent/channels/github.ts) and a turborepo-ai-agents crate in Cargo.toml — the detector likely only scans CI-workflow files and misses this standalone agent-app infrastructure.

The "versioned DB migrations" signal is likely a false positive for the core pipeline — this is a Rust build-system monorepo with no apparent database backend, so the match probably comes from one of the bundled example apps rather than reflecting turborepo's own delivery pipeline.

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security
dimensions.summary: Security posture is a deliberate mix of very strong and clearly unaddressed controls. Branch protection (10/10), dangerous-workflow hygiene (10/10), automated dependency updates (10/10), and signed releases/provenance (10/10) are all maxed out. But token permissions are weak (1.7/10 — only 4 of 23 workflows set an explicit permissions: scope, and one grants broad write), action pinning is weak (3.4/10 — only 32 of 95 action refs pinned by SHA/digest), there is no SAST wired into CI (0/10), and no SBOM is generated (0/10). The security policy itself is inherited from the org level rather than defined in-repo (8/10). This posture score is fixed at 64 and exposure is unknown since dependency vulnerabilities weren't inspected.

roadmap.title: Most CI workflows run without an explicit permissions: scope, and one grants broad write
roadmap.rationale: Broad default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions widen the blast radius if any of the 23 workflows or their third-party actions were ever compromised — a real concern for a platform this widely depended on, especially since deploy automation is already highly automated.
explore: What would it take to make a scoped `permissions:` block (or `permissions: {}` plus per-job opt-in) the default across workflows?
Which of the 23 workflows genuinely need write access, and could those be isolated and reviewed more tightly than the rest?

roadmap.title: Two-thirds of third-party Actions are pinned by tag rather than SHA
roadmap.rationale: Tag-pinned actions can be silently mutated upstream, letting a compromised marketplace action run in CI with repo secrets even though releases themselves are already signed and provenance-tracked — SHA-pinning closes that gap cheaply.
explore: The commit history shows at least one SHA re-pin already happening (rust-toolchain) — would it make sense to extend that practice to the rest of the 95 action references?
Is there appetite for a Renovate/Dependabot rule that keeps SHA pins current automatically, so pinning doesn't become stale maintenance burden?

roadmap.title: No static analysis (SAST) currently runs in CI
roadmap.rationale: Without CodeQL/Semgrep-style scanning gating merges, security-relevant patterns rely entirely on human review — a gap that stands out given how much else in this pipeline (release, deploy, review bots) is already automated.
explore: What's kept CodeQL or Semgrep out of the pipeline so far — cost, noise, or just not yet prioritized?
Could a SAST pass start as advisory-only (non-blocking) to build trust before it gates merges?

roadmap.title: Sampled tests lean toward thin 'did it deploy' smoke checks rather than behavioral assertions
roadmap.rationale: With 8593 test files and a 3.99 test-to-source ratio, the raw numbers look excellent, but the sampled examples/__tests__ files assert nothing beyond a successful deploy call — if this pattern is common elsewhere, file count is a weaker confidence signal than it appears, which matters more as AI starts generating a larger share of test code.
explore: Is the shallow example-deploy smoke pattern representative of test depth elsewhere (e.g. packages/cli/test/unit), or is it specific to a low-risk directory?
Would it be worth sampling assertion density in a couple of core packages to see whether this pattern holds broadly?

roadmap.title: AI-authored PRs are still a small share of volume, and whether they're reviewed as rigorously as human PRs isn't yet measurable
roadmap.rationale: The review/CI harness (CODEOWNERS, required approvals, status checks) is clearly ready for more agent-driven volume, so the current 5% AI-PR rate looks more like a team choice than an infrastructure gap — but until volume grows, it's hard to confirm AI PRs are held to the same bar as human ones.
explore: What would need to be true for the team to feel comfortable routing more categories of change through agents like Claude or Codex?
Would a lightweight tag on AI-authored PRs make it easier to track whether they're reviewed as rigorously as human-authored ones over time?

discrepancies.claim: The 5 sampled test files are all example-deployment smoke tests (examples/__tests__/integration/*.test.ts) asserting only that deployExample() resolves, so the reported '0 substantive assertions' likely reflects an unrepresentative sample rather than the true depth of the 8593-file suite, given AGENTS.md and CODEOWNERS reference a much larger per-package unit-test layer (e.g. packages/cli/test/unit/commands/*) that wasn't sampled.

The D1 signalScore of 58 may understate agent-guidance maturity: sampled evidence shows a hierarchical system (root AGENTS.md, package-scoped packages/cli/AGENTS.md with explicit task routing, examples/nextjs/AGENTS.md, a CLAUDE.md that @-imports AGENTS.md, and a dedicated .agents/skills/cli-ux/SKILL.md library) — nested scoping, skills, and @-imports are advanced techniques the flat signal may not fully credit.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions
dimensions.summary: Both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are present with nearly identical, substantive content: the tool stack (uv, ruff, mypy), a full script suite (test.sh, lint.sh, typecheck.sh, fix.sh), a documented workspace task system (scripts/poe), and explicit commit-message rules. This gives an agent concrete, runnable verify-after-change commands and clear constraints rather than a token stub. It falls short of the deepest tier of guidance, though — there is no mention of subagents, MCP servers, hooks, slash commands, or skills, and a commit ("add .claude to .gitignore #145") indicates any richer local Claude Code configuration is deliberately kept out of the tracked repo.
strengths: Two parallel, substantive guidance files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) with concrete build/test/lint/typecheck commands
Documents a shared workspace task system (scripts/poe/poe.toml) so guidance generalizes across sub-packages
Explicit, opinionated constraints (commit title/body format, explicit ban on Co-Authored-By trailers)
Concrete runnable examples (e.g. `./scripts/test.sh tests/unit/test_time.py -- -k coerce_duration`)
gaps: No coverage of subagents, MCP servers, hooks, slash commands, or skills
No explicit tool-permission policy for agents
.claude/ is gitignored (#145), so deeper local agent config isn't visible to new contributors or the detector
No architecture map orienting an agent to the codebase's module structure

dimensions.name: Automated Testing
dimensions.summary: The suite is genuinely substantial: 71 test files against source yield a healthy 0.44 test-to-source ratio, with pytest plus pytest-asyncio, pytest-xdist, hypothesis (property-based testing), respx, trio, and uvloop as dev dependencies — indicating deliberate coverage of async code paths and edge cases rather than superficial happy-path tests. conftest.py shows disciplined fixture hygiene (credential clearing, mock fixtures) and a `live` marker separates tests requiring real API credentials. No evidence of e2e, mutation, contract, or accessibility testing was found, which would be the next tier of rigor for an SDK with a public network-facing surface.
strengths: 71 test files with a healthy 0.44 test-to-source ratio
Property-based testing via hypothesis, plus async-specific tooling (pytest-asyncio, trio, uvloop)
Disciplined fixtures in conftest.py (env isolation, credential mocking)
Example tests are deliberately separated from unit tests (test.sh excludes example tests; test-examples.sh runs them in parallel)
gaps: No e2e/browser testing detected (not obviously needed for an SDK, but no smoke-test equivalent either)
No mutation testing (Stryker/mutmut) to validate test effectiveness
No API-schema/contract validation despite this being an API client SDK
No visible coverage-threshold enforcement (e.g. codecov gate) tying coverage to merge

dimensions.name: CI/CD & Delivery
dimensions.summary: CI is mature for the repo's scope: 4 GitHub Actions workflows cover linting, type-checking, testing, and an automated deploy step, and workflows consistently declare explicit least-privilege `permissions:` blocks. Note the signal's "policy-as-code (OPA/conftest)" detection is likely a mislabel — the actual tool is zizmor (a GitHub Actions workflow security linter run via `poe lint-zizmor`), not general policy-as-code like OPA/conftest evaluating Terraform/K8s manifests (see discrepancies). There's no IaC, GitOps, or progressive-delivery evidence, which is reasonable for a client SDK with no deployed service of its own, and no versioned DB migrations apply either.
strengths: 4 GitHub Actions workflows covering lint, typecheck, test, and deploy
CI enforces linting and an automated deploy step
Actions pinned by SHA/digest (8/8) and explicit permissions scopes (4/4 workflows)
Branch protection requires PR + 1 approval + code-owner review + signed commits + linear history
gaps: "Policy-as-code (OPA/conftest)" signal appears to be zizmor (workflow security linting), not true policy-as-code
No required status checks configured on the branch protection ruleset (process signals show status checks: no)
No IaC/GitOps/progressive-delivery evidence (may be out of scope for a client SDK)
No changesets/semantic-release visible for the deploy step's versioning discipline

dimensions.name: Agentic Workflows
dimensions.summary: No agentic workflow evidence was found anywhere in the sampled material: no AI review bots (CodeRabbit, Claude/Copilot review, Greptile), no LLM steps inside CI, no auto-fix/auto-PR bots, and no Renovate/Dependabot automation. This is corroborated by the process signals showing a 0% AI-involved PR rate. Despite strong human-guided AI tooling (D1) and a disciplined human review process, none of that AI usage has been embedded into the pipeline itself — every AI contribution today still depends entirely on a human to invoke, review, and merge it.
evidence: No agentic/AI-in-CI workflows detected (e.g. AI review bots, LLM steps in CI, auto-merge)
gaps: No AI code-review bot wired into pull requests
No LLM invocations inside CI workflows
No auto-fix or auto-PR tooling
No dependency-update automation (Renovate/Dependabot) with or without auto-merge

dimensions.name: Documentation & Knowledge
dimensions.summary: The README is substantial and well-organized (2092 chars, 4 sections: getting started, usage, public API vs internals), and a rich examples/ directory demonstrates real usage patterns (blob storage, multipart uploads, OIDC + cache middleware, sandbox PTY sessions). Notably, the sample also surfaced a genuine architecture decision record (src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md) documenting API design rationale — a signal of documentation maturity the deterministic score likely undercounts because it sits outside a canonical docs/adr/ path (see discrepancies). Still, no CONTRIBUTING.md, CHANGELOG.md, or a general /docs directory was found, so most institutional knowledge beyond the README and this one ADR isn't captured in a discoverable place.
strengths: Substantial, well-structured README with a working end-to-end usage example
Rich examples/ directory spanning blob storage, sandbox, OIDC, and cache use cases
A real ADR (src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md) documenting API design decisions and rationale
README explicitly documents the public-API-vs-internals boundary for consumers
gaps: No CONTRIBUTING.md found to guide human or agent contributors
No CHANGELOG.md despite being a versioned, published SDK
No general /docs directory; the one ADR found lives outside a canonical docs/adr/ path
No generated API reference (OpenAPI/typedoc-equivalent) despite being a typed SDK

dimensions.name: Code Quality & Guardrails
dimensions.summary: Guardrails are enforced, not just present: ruff handles linting/formatting, mypy (with a stricter per-module override for the `unstable` namespace) handles type-checking, and zizmor lints workflow files for security issues, all wired into the poe task runner. Process signals show these guardrails are actually gating merges in practice — 100% of merged PRs were reviewed, PRs require 1 approval plus code-owner sign-off, and 65% of merges were small-batch. No pre-commit hook config or CODEOWNERS-derived PR template was directly sampled, but the code-owner review requirement implies CODEOWNERS exists.
evidence: PR review coverage 100% (33 merged · 65% small · 0% reverted)
Pull requests required to merge (1 approval(s) + code owners)
strengths: ruff (lint + format) and mypy (with stricter rules for unstable modules) enforced via CI scripts
zizmor adds workflow-specific static analysis on top of code linting
100% PR review coverage and required code-owner approval before merge
65% small-PR rate and 0% revert rate indicate guardrails are working in practice, not just configured
gaps: No pre-commit hook config (.pre-commit-config.yaml, husky/lint-staged) sampled
No commitlint/conventional-commit enforcement despite commit-message guidance in AGENTS.md
Required status checks are not enabled on the branch ruleset per process signals
No PR template evidence sampled

dimensions.name: Commit & Velocity Signals
dimensions.summary: Recent commit history (30 commits analyzed) shows active, steady cadence and the repo was pushed within the last 30 days, but there is no AI co-authorship signal in the history. This is not necessarily an absence of AI use — AGENTS.md explicitly instructs contributors to "not include any Co-Authored-By line," meaning any AI involvement in commits is intentionally scrubbed from attribution. That's a defensible stylistic choice, but it also means D7's commit-based signal structurally cannot detect AI-native workflow adoption here, and the org has no other visible mechanism (labels, PR metadata) to track how much of the codebase is AI-assisted.
strengths: Active, consistent commit cadence (30 recent commits, pushed within 30 days)
Commit messages follow a disciplined, documented format (title ≤50 chars, wrapped body, what+why)
PR-based workflow (not direct pushes) for essentially all changes sampled
gaps: No AI co-author trailers found — but this is a deliberate policy (AGENTS.md bans Co-Authored-By), not necessarily low AI usage
No alternative mechanism (labels, PR metadata) to audit how much of the codebase is AI-assisted
No conventional-commit prefix enforcement visible in the sampled messages

dimensions.name: AI Process & Harness
dimensions.summary: There is no dedicated AI process harness: no evals/golden-test directory for LLM or agent output, no structured prompt/agent library beyond the two guidance files, and no agent-specific runbooks were found in a canonical location. The one ADR discovered (src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md) is exactly the kind of agent-readable operational documentation this dimension rewards, but as a single file outside a docs/adr/ convention it's easy for a path-based detector to miss (see discrepancies) and doesn't by itself constitute a repeatable harness. The strong human PR-review gate (100% reviewed, code-owner approval, signed commits) substitutes for a structured AI-verification harness today, but that's a manual control, not a repeatable AI-specific one.
evidence: No dedicated AI process/harness detected (e.g. evals, prompt library, agent runbooks)
strengths: CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md give agents a repeatable command surface (test/lint/typecheck/fix scripts)
A real ADR (src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md) exists as agent-readable design documentation
Signed commits and an 11-rule branch protection ruleset add governance around what reaches main
100% PR-review coverage functions as a de facto human verification gate for any AI-assisted change
gaps: No evals or golden-test directory for AI/LLM output
No structured prompt/agent library (no prompts/, agents/, or .claude/agents/ with multiple specs)
The single ADR found isn't part of a systematic docs/adr/ or runbook convention
No documented Definition-of-Done or agent-specific contribution checklist beyond commit-message rules

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security
dimensions.summary: Security posture scores 60/100 on the deterministic check battery, with exposure unrated because dependencies weren't inspected. The repo does several supply-chain fundamentals well: branch protection is strong (protected, 1 approval, code-owner review, signed commits — 8/10), no dangerous workflow patterns like script injection or untrusted checkout were found (10/10), all 4 workflows declare explicit least-privilege permissions (10/10), and all 8 sampled action references are pinned by SHA/digest (10/10). It inherits an org-level SECURITY.md rather than a repo-local one (8/10). The gaps are concentrated and high-impact: no SAST tool (CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar) is wired into CI (0/10), no dependency-update automation like Dependabot/Renovate is committed (0/10), no artifact signing or provenance attestation exists for releases (0/10), and no SBOM is generated (0/10).
evidence: Branch protection [posture/high]: 8/10 — Default branch: protected, 1 approval(s), code-owner review, signed commits.
Dangerous workflow [posture/critical]: 10/10 — No script-injection or untrusted-checkout patterns detected.
Token permissions [posture/high]: 10/10 — 4/4 workflows set an explicit `permissions:` scope.
SAST [posture/medium]: 0/10 — No SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar) wired into CI.
Dependency updates [posture/high]: 0/10 — No dependency-update tool committed.
Pinned dependencies [posture/medium]: 10/10 — 8/8 Actions/images pinned by SHA/digest (8 action refs).
Security policy [posture/medium]: 8/10 — Inherits an org-level SECURITY.md (no repo-local policy).
Signed releases [posture/high]: 0/10 — No artifact signing / provenance in CI.
Known vulnerabilities [exposure/high]: n/a/10 — Dependency vulnerabilities not inspected (no lockfile / no alert access).
strengths: Strong branch protection: required approval, code-owner review, signed commits, linear history
No dangerous workflow patterns (script injection, untrusted checkout) detected across CI
All 4 workflows scope explicit least-privilege `permissions:` blocks
100% of sampled Actions are pinned by SHA/digest rather than mutable tags
gaps: Add CodeQL (or Semgrep) scanning that runs on pull_request.
Add a `.github/dependabot.yml` (or Renovate) config.
Sign releases with cosign and emit SLSA provenance (actions/attest).
Generate an SBOM (Syft/CycloneDX) on release.

report.headline: vercel-py has a genuinely AI-native foundation — dual CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md guidance, a rigorous async-aware test suite, and a disciplined, gated review/CI process — but AI participation stops at the human keyboard: nothing in the pipeline yet reviews, verifies, or ships changes autonomously.
strengths: Dual CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files give agents concrete, runnable build/test/lint/typecheck commands and explicit commit conventions, not just a token stub
A rigorous test suite (71 files, 0.44 ratio) that goes beyond happy-path checks with property-based testing (hypothesis) and dedicated async tooling (trio, uvloop, pytest-asyncio)
CI enforces real guardrails end-to-end: linting, type-checking, and a workflow security linter (zizmor) gate 4 pipelines, with all Actions pinned by SHA and scoped least-privilege permissions
A disciplined human review culture: 100% of merged PRs are reviewed, code-owner approval and signed commits are required, and 65% of PRs are small-batch
Documentation goes a step past the README — a genuine ADR (src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md) and a rich, working examples/ directory demonstrate real design rationale and usage patterns
risks: Zero agentic automation in the delivery pipeline (D4=0) — no AI review bots, no LLM-in-CI steps, no auto-fix/auto-PR loops — so today's AI usage stays individual and manual rather than compounding across the team

No dependency-update automation and no SAST tool wired into CI, leaving stale/vulnerable dependencies and common code-security issues as blind spots despite otherwise strong branch-protection and pinning discipline

No dedicated AI process harness (evals, prompt library, agent runbooks) exists beyond CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, so there's no repeatable, verifiable system governing AI contributions beyond standard human PR review
Institutional knowledge beyond the README and one ADR is thin — no CONTRIBUTING.md or CHANGELOG.md — limiting how easily an agent or new contributor can self-orient
AGENTS.md's explicit ban on Co-Authored-By trailers means AI involvement is invisible in commit history, removing a signal the team could otherwise use to gauge and govern its own AI adoption

roadmap.title: Agents write code but nothing yet reviews or ships it autonomously
roadmap.rationale: With zero AI review bots or LLM steps in CI, every AI-assisted change still depends entirely on a human reviewer to catch issues — the workflow can't yet compound the way it would with an automated first-pass review loop in place.
explore: What would it look like to trial an AI review bot (e.g. a Claude Code review action, CodeRabbit) on a subset of PRs before considering it more broadly?
Which categories of PR — docs, small fixes, dependency bumps — feel low-risk enough to let an agent triage or pre-review first?

roadmap.title: There's no dedicated harness for verifying AI-generated changes beyond ordinary code review
roadmap.rationale: CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md tell agents how to work, but there's no evals/golden-test layer or agent runbook that would let the team check AI output systematically rather than relying solely on a human catching issues each time.
explore: Would it help to capture a few 'golden' example tasks that any new agent workflow gets checked against before the team trusts it more broadly?
Is there a recurring category of AI-produced change where a lightweight eval could catch regressions earlier than review currently does?

roadmap.title: Dependency freshness and code-level security scanning rely on someone noticing, not automation
roadmap.rationale: No Dependabot/Renovate config and no SAST tool (CodeQL/Semgrep) are wired into CI, so vulnerable or stale dependencies and common code-security issues could linger — a gap the strong branch-protection and pinning practices elsewhere don't otherwise cover.
explore: Would turning on Dependabot security updates or a CodeQL workflow fit naturally alongside the existing 4 CI workflows?
Has dependency scanning been left out deliberately, or is it just something that hasn't reached the top of the list yet?

roadmap.title: AI's fingerprint is deliberately erased from commit history
roadmap.rationale: AGENTS.md instructs contributors to omit Co-Authored-By trailers, which keeps history tidy but also means there's no way to see, in aggregate, how much of the codebase is AI-assisted — a signal that could otherwise help the team calibrate trust and review depth as AI use grows.
explore: Would some lightweight marker (even just in PR descriptions, not commits) help the team see its own AI-adoption curve without cluttering history?
Is hiding AI attribution a considered choice to avoid noise, or worth revisiting now that AI-assisted contributions are routine?

roadmap.title: Knowledge beyond the README lives in one ADR and the code itself
roadmap.rationale: Aside from a strong README and one ADR, there's no CONTRIBUTING.md, CHANGELOG, or docs/adr directory — architecture decisions and contribution norms aren't consistently captured somewhere agents or new contributors would reliably find them.
explore: Would formalizing the ADR pattern already used in src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md into a repo-wide docs/adr/ folder make past decisions easier to rediscover?
Is a CHANGELOG or CONTRIBUTING.md something worth considering, given this SDK is public-facing with 145+ PRs of history?

discrepancies.claim: The D3 signal's "Policy-as-code (OPA/conftest)" detection is likely a mislabel of zizmor — a GitHub Actions workflow security linter run via `poe lint-zizmor` and listed as a dev dependency (`zizmor>=1.24.1`) in pyproject.toml — rather than true policy-as-code (OPA/conftest evaluating Terraform/K8s-style manifests).

D5's signalScore of 35 does not appear to credit the genuine ADR found at src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md (a substantive architecture decision record documenting the unstable SDK API design), suggesting the documentation-depth signal undercounts due to the file living outside a canonical docs/adr/ path.

D8 explicitly rewards "agent-readable operational docs/runbooks/ADRs," but its signalScore of 11 shows no ADR detection despite src/vercel/unstable/ADR.md existing in the sampled files, suggesting the detector's path patterns missed it.

level.name: Integrated
level.tagline: Agents in the loop, not just at the keyboard
level.description: Agents are embedded in the process: AI code review, AI steps in CI, auto-fix/auto-PR, and dependency automation. Strong docs (including docs for agents), observability, and reliable CI/CD let autonomy compound.

posture.label: AI-Native
posture.blurb: Adopting AI with the engineering rigor to ship it safely.

dimensions.name: AI Tooling & Conventions
dimensions.summary: The repository has best-in-class, duplicated-for-redundancy agent guidance: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md carry identical, detailed content covering architecture (core, next, cli, world/world-local/world-vercel, swc-plugin-workflow, workbench examples), the workflow/step execution model, explicit critical rules ('never push to main/stable', preserve agent-discoverable doc routes), and workspace-level build/test/e2e/bench commands. .cursor/rules/*.mdc adds scoped, task-specific playbooks (a real end-to-end deploy-and-curl-test procedure, SWC plugin test/update-fixture instructions), and a .claude/ directory is present. This is guidance an agent could actually execute against, not a token stub.
evidence: References advanced agent tooling (MCP / hooks / subagents)
strengths: CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md document a concrete architecture map across every package plus the workflow/step execution model
Explicit 'CRITICAL RULES' constraints (never push to main/stable; preserve agent-facing doc sitemap routes)
.cursor/rules/workflow-deployment.mdc gives a full runnable deploy-and-verify loop (turbo build, vc deploy --prebuilt, curl trigger, inspect URL)
Coverage of build/test/typecheck/e2e/bench commands at workspace and package granularity
gaps: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are verbatim duplicates, creating a drift risk if one is updated without the other
No MCP server configuration was visible in the sampled excerpts despite the 'advanced tooling' signal
No visible slash-commands/skills directory contents to confirm depth beyond Cursor rules and .claude/

dimensions.name: Automated Testing
dimensions.summary: Testing is deep and systemic: 469 test files against a 0.47 test-to-source ratio, a configured framework (Vitest with @vitest/coverage-v8) and coverage tracking, and sampled tests carry substantive behavioral assertions rather than smoke checks. package.json scripts reveal deliberate rigor beyond unit tests — a dedicated e2e suite, a race-condition regression repro harness (test:e2e:event-log-race-repro), staged Next.js webpack tests, and a vitest bench harness — reflecting a test philosophy built around this SDK's hardest problem (deterministic replay under failure).
evidence: Sampled tests assert behavior (37 substantive assertions across 4 sampled test file(s))
strengths: 469 test files with a healthy 0.47 test-to-source ratio and confirmed substantive assertions
Dedicated e2e and race-condition regression-repro test suites (event-log-race-repro) targeting the durable-replay core
Coverage tooling configured (@vitest/coverage-v8)
Custom benchmark harness (vitest bench) for performance regression awareness
gaps: No evidence of mutation testing (Stryker/mutmut) to validate assertion strength
No accessibility (axe/pa11y) or API-schema validation (Schemathesis/Spectral) tooling surfaced
No contract-testing (Pact) evidence for the world/world-vercel backend boundary
Rust workspace (swc-plugin-workflow) test coverage isn't clearly reflected in the reported ratio

dimensions.name: CI/CD & Delivery
dimensions.summary: Delivery is fully gated and automated: 13 GitHub Actions workflows run lint, test, and build; changesets (@changesets/cli, changelog-github) drive automated versioning/release and changelog generation; deploys are automated; DB/event-log migrations are versioned; and status checks are required to merge. This is a pipeline mature enough that an agent could safely propose and land changes behind real gates, not just a CI badge.
strengths: 13 CI workflows covering lint, test, build, and release
Changesets-driven automated release and changelog generation, including a custom check-release-major script enforcing version consistency across packages
Automated deploy step and versioned Postgres/event-log migrations
Required status checks and branch protection gate every merge
gaps: No Terraform/CDK/Pulumi-style IaC evidence sampled
No progressive-delivery or feature-flag SDK evidence
Token-permission scoping across workflows is weak (see D9), undercutting the 'safe for an agent to drive' bar despite strong functional gating

dimensions.name: Agentic Workflows
dimensions.summary: An AI code-review agent and an LLM invocation inside CI are wired into the pipeline alongside issue/PR automation, which is genuine agentic-workflow investment. However, the sampled PR history (40 of 2387 PRs) shows a 0% AI-involved rate, and no dependency-update bot (Renovate/Dependabot) is committed at all — so while the scaffolding for an autonomous review/fix loop exists, its real footprint in shipped changes is not yet visible in the evidence provided.
evidence: AI code-review agent in the pipeline
strengths: AI code-review agent present in the CI pipeline
LLM invocation inside a CI workflow (beyond simple keyboard-assist tooling)
Issue-to-PR automation workflow configured
gaps: 0% AI-involvement measured across the sampled 40 merged/open PRs, despite bot tooling being wired in
No Renovate/Dependabot (or equivalent) auto-merge automation committed for dependency PRs
No visible evidence of an autonomous fix-and-reopen loop (auto-fix bot) distinct from review commentary

dimensions.name: Documentation & Knowledge
dimensions.summary: Documentation is broader and more deliberately agent-aware than the raw signal fully captures: beyond the substantial README, dedicated /docs, and changesets-based changelog, the sampled docs use a structured content model (frontmatter with title/description/type/prerequisites/related-links) and AGENTS.md explicitly protects an agent-discoverable llms.mdx sitemap route — meaning docs are treated as a first-class interface for both humans and agents. dimensions.name: Code Quality & Guardrails
dimensions.summary: Guardrails are enforced, not just present: Biome provides a comprehensive, opinionated lint+format configuration with several rules escalated to error, husky + lint-staged runs formatting pre-commit, CODEOWNERS and a PR template exist, and branch protection requires 1 approval plus code-owner review before merge — reflected in a 100% reviewed-merge rate. dimensions.name: AI Process & Harness
dimensions.summary: The repository shows a genuine harness around AI usage rather than ad hoc prompting: an AI-output eval/golden-test harness, a structured prompt/agent library, an AI-aware contribution process (PR template / definition-of-done), and a strongly protected default branch (8 ruleset rules, signed commits) that gates any change including AI-authored ones. The main open question is how heavily this harness is actually exercised, given how little AI involvement shows up in the sampled PR history.

Inherits an org-level SECURITY.md security policy (8/10)
gaps: Add CodeQL (or Semgrep) scanning that runs on pull_request.
Add a `.github/dependabot.yml` (or Renovate) config.
Sign releases with cosign and emit SLSA provenance (actions/attest).
Generate an SBOM (Syft/CycloneDX) on release.
Add a least-privilege top-level `permissions:` block (default `contents: read`) to every workflow.
Pin third-party Actions to a full commit SHA (and container images to a digest).

report.headline: vercel/workflow runs a genuinely AI-native engineering loop — deep, duplicated-for-redundancy agent guidance, a 469-file test suite with a race-condition regression harness, and a fully gated 13-workflow CI/CD pipeline — but the software-supply-chain layer (SAST, dependency scanning, signing, SBOM, token scoping) hasn't caught up, and the sampled PR history shows the AI-review tooling isn't yet visibly load-bearing.
strengths: Exceptional, technique-rich agent guidance (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/Cursor rules) with a real architecture map, explicit constraints, and an executable deploy-and-verify playbook
Large, purpose-built test suite (469 files, 0.47 ratio) including a dedicated event-log race-condition regression harness — evidence of testing built around the system's actual failure modes
Fully gated delivery pipeline: 13 CI workflows, required status checks, signed commits, code-owner review, and changesets-driven automated release/changelog
Fast, disciplined review cadence (median 2h time-to-merge, 63% small PRs, 100% reviewed-merge rate)
Documentation treated as an agent-facing interface, not just a human one — AGENTS.md explicitly protects the llms.mdx agent-discoverable doc sitemap
risks: Supply-chain security posture is the clear outlier (D9=46): no SAST, no dependency-update automation, minimal Action pinning, no signing or SBOM — a real gap for a widely-depended-on SDK (2184 stars)
CI workflows are broadly over-permissioned (only 2 of 11 scope `permissions:`, 2 grant broad write), raising blast radius if any Action or dependency is compromised
AI review/automation tooling exists in the pipeline, but the sampled 40-PR history shows 0% AI involvement — the autonomous loop's real-world footprint is unproven at scale
CODEOWNERS is a single repo-wide wildcard rather than path-scoped, limiting targeted review guardrails as the multi-package monorepo grows
Conventional-commit adoption is partial (43%) with no enforcement, leaving commit-based automation reliant on manual discipline

roadmap.title: Supply-chain verification (SAST, signing, SBOM) isn't yet part of the pipeline that otherwise gates every merge
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection and workflow hygiene are excellent, but nothing in CI currently checks code for vulnerabilities, scans dependencies for known CVEs, or signs what gets released — for a durable-execution SDK many other systems will depend on, an unnoticed vulnerable dependency or unsigned artifact could travel further before anyone caught it.
explore: If a dependency shipped a known CVE tomorrow, how would the team currently find out?
What would it take to see a SAST pass light up on every PR as routinely as the test suite does today?
Would signing releases change how confidently downstream teams adopt an update from this SDK?

roadmap.title: Most CI workflows run without declaring what they're allowed to touch
roadmap.rationale: Only 2 of 11 workflows set an explicit `permissions:` scope and 2 grant broad write access — as more automation (bots, LLM-invoking steps) runs inside CI, an unscoped token turns any single compromised step or dependency into a much bigger incident than it needs to be.
explore: What's the minimum permission each workflow actually needs to do its job?
Would a repo-wide default-deny `permissions: {}` with per-job opt-ins change how comfortable the team feels running unfamiliar Actions?

roadmap.title: AI review/automation is wired into CI, but merged-PR history doesn't yet show it landing changes
roadmap.rationale: An AI code-review bot and an LLM step inside CI are real investments, and 8 of the last 30 commits carry AI/bot attribution — but the sampled 40-PR window shows 0% AI involvement, and no dependency-update bot exists to auto-merge routine upgrades. That combination makes it hard to tell whether the autonomous loop is a proven, everyday part of how change ships or still mostly latent.
explore: Where does the AI review bot's feedback actually surface on a PR — visible enough that contributors treat it as a real signal, not background noise?
Would tracking AI-authored/AI-reviewed merge rates over time help the team see whether this trend is growing or stalled?
Is there an appetite for a dependency-update bot (Renovate/Dependabot) as a low-risk first autonomous-merge loop to build confidence from?

roadmap.title: Ownership and commit-convention guardrails are coarse-grained for a monorepo this size
roadmap.rationale: CODEOWNERS currently applies one wildcard rule to the entire repo, and only 43% of commits follow a conventional format with nothing enforcing it — as the package count grows (core, next, cli, world, world-local, world-vercel, swc-plugin, workbench apps), finer-grained ownership and commit structure make it easier for both humans and agents to route changes to the right reviewers and automate changelogs reliably.
explore: Would path-scoped CODEOWNERS entries per package change who gets pulled into review, and would that be an improvement?
Is the current 43% conventional-commit rate a deliberate choice, or something worth tightening with a commit-lint check?

discrepancies.claim: D5's signalScore of 60 may undercount documentation maturity — the sampled docs use a structured content model (typed frontmatter with prerequisites/related cross-links) and AGENTS.md explicitly protects an agent-discoverable llms.mdx sitemap route, indicating docs deliberately built for both humans and agents beyond a generic 'README + docs + changelog' read.

The process-signal figure of 0% AI-involved PRs (across the 40-PR sample) appears inconsistent with D7's commit-level signal of 8 of 30 recent commits being AI/bot-attributed; this may reflect different detection windows (PR metadata vs. commit trailers) rather than an actual absence of AI participation, and is worth reconciling rather than taken at face value.
